title: Optimal fidelity over zero-capacity erasure channels
authors: Camilo Castro-Landolt, Rabsan Galib Ahmed, Graeme Smith
problem: An erasure channel delivers a quantum system intact with probability \(\gamma\) and otherwise replaces it by a flag that says it was lost. For \(\gamma\le1/2\) the environment receives at least as much as the receiver, so the channel's quantum capacity is zero: no code transmits qubits at a positive rate. Yet a single \(d\)-dimensional system can still be sent with some fidelity, and spreading it over many channel uses can improve that fidelity. How well can a fixed-size quantum system be transmitted through arbitrarily many uses of such a channel?
result: For every logical dimension \(d\ge2\) and transmission probability \(0<\gamma\le1/2\), the best entanglement fidelity achievable with any number of channel uses is at most \(\gamma+(1-\gamma)/d\), and this value is reached as the number of uses grows. The upper bound comes from fractional extendibility of the channel; the matching code encodes each logical label in a mixture of a repetition state and single-excitation Dicke states, with the mixing weight \(t^\star=1/(1+(d-1)\gamma)\).
significance: Zero capacity says that the rate must vanish; this result says exactly what fidelity survives at vanishing rate. For a qubit at \(\gamma=0.35\), one use of the channel gives at best 0.5125, while many uses approach 0.675, and nothing does better. The upper-bound technique, which turns recovery from disjoint subsets of an extension into a graph-theoretic overlap bound, applies to any channel with a fractional extension.
limitations: The optimum is asymptotic, and the achieving code needs many channel uses for each logical system; the convergence rate was not optimized. The bound concerns entanglement fidelity, an average over inputs, rather than worst-case fidelity. Only erasure channels are solved; other antidegradable channels remain open. The authors note a recent independent work by Gamal and coauthors with a similar bound. They state that AI tools assisted a numerical search for promising codes in June 2026, in an early special case, and that all analytical work was done by the authors.
summary_basis: Description based on the full arXiv HTML of v1, read 2026-11-25: Secs. I–IV, including Theorem 3, Corollary 4, the code of Eq. (16), the decoder, Propositions 5–8 and Theorem 9. The appendix calculations were not read. Editorial checks: exact simulation of the code and decoder for (n, d, j) = (7, 2, 3), (8, 2, 4), (6, 3, 3) and (7, 3, 3) reproduced Proposition 8 to ten digits; maximizing f_t(γ) over t gives γ + (1 − γ)/d at t* in all tested cases; averaging over the binomial erasure number gives 0.6738, 0.6749 and 0.67499 for n = 50, 500 and 5000 at d = 2, γ = 0.35, approaching 0.675. The norm identity of Lemma 10, ‖Π_S Π_T‖ = 1/d, was checked numerically for d = 2, 3, 4.

methods_basis: Based on the linked paper version. Derivations marked as editorial, and suggested uses in other problems, are editorial guidance rather than results of the paper.
description: The erasure channel acts as \(\mathcal E_\gamma(\rho)=\gamma\rho+(1-\gamma)\ket e\bra e\). It is antidegradable for \(\gamma\le1/2\): the environment can simulate what the receiver gets, so perfect recovery would let two parties hold the same quantum information, which no-cloning forbids. Strong converse theorems add that at any fixed positive rate the fidelity of every code decays exponentially. They say nothing about a fixed logical system sent through more and more uses of the channel, where the rate tends to zero.

The paper answers that question exactly for entanglement fidelity, the overlap of the output with a maximally entangled state when half of it is sent. One use of the channel with the best decoder gives \(\gamma+(1-\gamma)/d^2\). With \(n\) uses and arbitrary encoding and decoding, the fidelity never exceeds \(\gamma+(1-\gamma)/d\), and a family of permutation-invariant codes reaches that value as \(n\to\infty\). The improvement replaces the \(1/d^2\) of random guessing by \(1/d\), the value obtained when the classical label is recovered but coherence is lost.

The upper bound uses fractional extendibility. An erasure channel with \(\gamma=q/(p+q)\) can be extended to \(p+q\) outputs so that any \(q\) of them reproduce the receiver's state. Two disjoint groups can then each recover the reference's partner, and the maximally entangled projectors for disjoint groups overlap by at most \(1/d\). A bound on how much weight a family of nearly orthogonal vectors can share with one vector, the approximate Lovász theta function of a Kneser graph, turns this into the fidelity bound.

The code balances two needs. Repetition states \(\ket a^{\otimes n}\) keep the label \(a\) on every system, so any survivor reveals it, but they lose all coherence when one system is erased. States with one excitation \(a\) on a background of another label keep coherence between labels when only background systems are lost. Mixing the two with the right weight makes the conditional fidelity, at the typical fraction \(\gamma\) of survivors, equal to the upper bound.

methods.technique: Fractional extendibility turned into a Kneser-graph overlap bound
methods.explanation: If the receiver's state can be rebuilt from any \(q\) of \(p+q\) extension systems, then disjoint groups give vectors that each overlap the global state as much as the true fidelity, yet overlap each other by at most \(1/d\). A theta-function bound limits how many such vectors can all lean towards one state.
math: Purify the extension and dilate each recovery map to a unitary \(U_S\). For every \(q\)-subset \(S\), the projector \(M_S=U_S^\dagger(\Phi_{RD_S}\otimes I)U_S\) satisfies \(\langle\tilde\sigma|M_S|\tilde\sigma\rangle=F\), the fidelity. Normalize \(\ket{v_S}=M_S\ket{\tilde\sigma}/\sqrt F\), so \(|\langle\tilde\sigma|v_S\rangle|^2=F\). For disjoint \(S,T\) the dilations commute and \(\|M_SM_T\|=\|\Pi_S\Pi_T\|=1/d\), because two maximally entangled projectors sharing the reference overlap with operator norm \(1/d\). Cauchy–Schwarz then gives \(|\langle v_S|v_T\rangle|\le1/d\).

The \(\ket{v_S}\) form a \(1/d\)-orthonormal representation of the Kneser graph \(KG_{p+q,q}\), whose vertices are the \(q\)-subsets and whose edges join disjoint ones. Using the known value of the approximate theta function, \[\binom{p+q}{q}F\le\vartheta_{1/d}(KG_{p+q,q})=\binom{p+q-1}{q-1}\Bigl(1+\frac{p}{qd}\Bigr),\] so \(F\le\frac{q}{p+q}+\frac{p}{d(p+q)}=\gamma+\frac{1-\gamma}{d}\).

Extendibility survives tensor powers and local operations, so the bound covers every encoder, every decoder and every number of uses. Irrational \(\gamma\) follow by composing erasure channels: \(\mathcal E_\gamma=\mathcal E_{\gamma/\gamma_m}\circ\mathcal E_{\gamma_m}\) for rational \(\gamma_m>\gamma\), and the extra erasure is absorbed into the decoder. Editorial check: \(\|\Pi_S\Pi_T\|=1/d\) was confirmed numerically for \(d=2,3,4\).
methods.transfer: Whenever a state can be reconstructed from several disjoint parts of an extension, the reconstruction projectors become nearly orthogonal vectors, and Lovász-type bounds cap the achievable overlap. This applies to other extendible channels and to bounds on approximate cloning or broadcasting.

methods.technique: Repetition plus single-excitation Dicke code, tuned by Cauchy–Schwarz
methods.explanation: Repetition protects the classical label and single excitations protect coherence. Conditioning the decoder on the number of erasures reduces the problem to one surviving fraction, and the best mixing weight follows from a one-line inequality.
math: The encoder is \[V\ket a=\sqrt t\,\ket{D^n(ne_a)}+\sqrt{\frac{1-t}{d-1}}\sum_{k\ne a}\ket{D^n(e_a+(n-1)e_k)},\] where \(\ket{D^n(\vec r)}\) is the qudit Dicke state with occupation numbers \(\vec r\). For \(n\ge3\) all occupation vectors are distinct, so \(V\) is an isometry. With \(j\) erasures, the decoder maps each surviving Dicke state with background \(i\) to its excitation label \(a\), and sends everything else to the maximally mixed state.

For \(3\le j\le n-3\) the paper finds the conditional fidelity \[F_{e}=\frac1d\Bigl[\sqrt t+\sqrt{(d-1)(1-t)x}\Bigr]^2,\qquad x=1-\frac jn.\] Cauchy–Schwarz on \((\sqrt t,\sqrt{1-t})\) and \((1,\sqrt{(d-1)x})\) gives \(F_e\le(1+(d-1)x)/d\), with equality at \(t=1/(1+(d-1)x)\). At the typical survival fraction \(x=\gamma\) this is \(\gamma+(1-\gamma)/d\), the upper bound.

Since the erasure flags reveal \(j\), Hoeffding's inequality concentrates \(j/n\) near \(1-\gamma\), and monotonicity of the conditional fidelity in \(x\) gives a lower bound that tends to the optimum. Editorial checks: an exact simulation of encoder, partial trace and decoder reproduced the formula for four choices of \((n,d,j)\); the binomial average for \(d=2\), \(\gamma=0.35\) rises from 0.6738 at \(n=50\) to 0.67499 at \(n=5000\).
methods.transfer: Mixing a component that protects populations with one that protects coherences, and choosing the weight by Cauchy–Schwarz at the typical noise level, is a simple design rule for approximate codes on any channel whose damage can be counted.
